clue.text: Estate needs to be settled without me

indicators.note: without in its old sense of outside: the jumbled letters sit around the other word
letters that are yet to be settled are not in their final order, so these are rearranged

explanation.surface: An estate owner is told the matter must be resolved without their involvement.
explanation.walkthrough: 'without' here means outside, not lacking: the anagram of NEEDS (from 'to be settled'), split DE...SNE, wraps ME.
explanation.definitionFit: A demesne is land held and worked by a lord, a landed property or domain.

clue.text: Agreeable chaps may do so, paradoxically

definitions.text: Agreeable chaps may do so, paradoxically

parts.words: Agreeable chaps may do so, paradoxically
parts.note: the stock phrase about friends who agree to disagree: agreeable people do the opposite of agreeing

explanation.surface: A wry remark about how friendly men behave.
explanation.definitionFit: To agree to disagree is a set phrase, so pleasant people paradoxically end up holding opposing views.

clue.text: Swallow one drink

parts.note: the martin is a bird of the swallow family
I is the Roman numeral for one

explanation.surface: Someone gulps down a single drink.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Swallow' reads as a verb but is the bird.
explanation.definitionFit: A martini is a cocktail of gin and vermouth.

clue.text: Temporary effect of education cuts?

explanation.surface: A question about what happens when school budgets are slashed.
explanation.walkthrough: The second reading splits the answer: cutting education might leave a school term that is shorter.
explanation.definitionFit: Short-term means lasting only a brief period; jokingly, a shortened school session.

clue.text: Host in disorderly retreat — nine or ten are inert

indicators.note: something disorderly is out of order, so these letters are jumbled

explanation.surface: A party host beats a messy retreat while the guests lie motionless.
explanation.walkthrough: 'disorderly' jumbles RETREAT and NINE; the setter adds a second route: 'ten are inert' is the same eleven letters, jumbled again.
explanation.definitionFit: An entertainer is one who hosts and amuses guests or an audience.

clue.text: Affinity for one of 10 when sailing

explanation.surface: A sense of fellow feeling is felt by a monarch at sea.
explanation.walkthrough: 10 is KINGS; one king at sea is aboard the king's ship, which runs together almost into the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: Kinship is a close relationship or feeling of connection; punningly, a monarch's vessel.

clue.text: It's not beyond him — that's understood

explanation.surface: Someone remarks that a task is within a man's powers, as all agree.
explanation.walkthrough: Something difficult is 'beyond my ken'; the answer is also a man's name, so 'him' fits the first reading.
explanation.definitionFit: Ken is a man's name and also means range of knowledge, so what is within it is understood.

clue.text: Like the truth about the emperor in his new suit?

definitions.text: Like the truth about the emperor in his new suit?

parts.words: Like the truth about the emperor in his new suit?
parts.note: the fairy tale of the emperor's invisible clothes, plus the set phrase for the plain, unvarnished truth

explanation.surface: A question about the fable of the vain emperor and his imaginary clothes.
explanation.definitionFit: The bare truth is a stock phrase, and the emperor in the tale wore nothing at all.

clue.text: County part, originally

parts.note: an old administrative division of an English shire, also a number

explanation.surface: A reference to how English shires were once divided.
explanation.walkthrough: In medieval England a shire was divided into units with their own courts, named after the number.
explanation.definitionFit: A historical subdivision of an English county was called by this numeral name.

clue.text: Means to admit request for drink

explanation.surface: Someone at dinner confesses a craving for wine.
explanation.walkthrough: The second reading splits the answer: 'pass (the) port', said round a dinner table.
explanation.definitionFit: A travel document grants entry to a country; and asking for fortified wine to be handed along the table.

clue.text: "Die two months ago, and not yet?" ( Hamlet )

definitions.text: "Die two months ago, and not yet?" ( Hamlet )

parts.words: "Die two months ago, and not yet?" ( Hamlet )
parts.note: a quotation from Shakespeare's play with one word missing; the missing word goes in the grid

explanation.surface: A line of Shakespeare with a gap to fill.
explanation.walkthrough: Hamlet says of his father, 'die two months ago, and not forgotten yet?'
explanation.definitionFit: The missing word in Hamlet's line means no longer remembered, out of mind.

clue.text: College men on board

explanation.surface: Members of a Cambridge college sit on a governing committee.
explanation.walkthrough: King's is a Cambridge college; 'men on board' are chess pieces.
explanation.definitionFit: King's College, Cambridge; and pieces on a chessboard, the royal figures.

clue.text: Old 20's book from this poet

parts.note: 20 is the marsupial answer elsewhere; the book is the cat poems collection by its American-born writer

explanation.surface: An old book from an earlier poet is mentioned.
explanation.walkthrough: 20-down is POSSUM, so the clue reads 'Old Possum's book', the poems on which the musical Cats was based.
explanation.definitionFit: T. S. Eliot wrote Old Possum's Book of Practical Cats, and Old Possum was his nickname.

clue.text: "Foggy" journey, for example?

parts.note: the Jules Verne hero who went around the world in eighty days, made an adjective

explanation.surface: A question about travelling through mist.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Foggy' means belonging to Phileas Fogg, who travelled round the world and came back to London.
explanation.definitionFit: Fogg's voyage ended where it started, a journey out and back again.

clue.text: Reserves needed for cup-tie — press confused

indicators.note: confused letters are mixed up, so these are rearranged

explanation.surface: Reporters are puzzled by the seat reservations for a knockout football match.
explanation.walkthrough: 'confused' jumbles CUPTIE and PRESS; 'needed for' links.
explanation.definitionFit: At auction the lowest price a seller will accept is the reserve, also called the upset price.

clue.text: Lady Jane Grey's 24 such a sensation

definitions.text: Lady Jane Grey's 24 such a sensation

parts.words: Lady Jane Grey's 24 such a sensation
parts.note: 24 is the rule answer; the Tudor claimant held the throne for a little over a week

explanation.surface: A remark that a Tudor queen's rule caused a stir.
explanation.walkthrough: 24-across is REIGN; Lady Jane Grey was queen of England for only nine days in 1553.
explanation.definitionFit: A brief marvel that is soon forgotten, like a reign lasting just over a week.

clue.text: Presage row within Irish political group

indicators.note: within says the row word sits inside the presage word

parts.note: a presage is a sign of what is to come, an omen
a row is a line, a range

explanation.surface: A forecast of a quarrel inside an Irish party.
explanation.walkthrough: 'row' suggests a quarrel but is a line.
explanation.definitionFit: The Orange Order is a Protestant fraternity in Northern Ireland whose members march each July.

clue.text: Coteries may be

indicators.note: the word could become something else when its letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: A remark about exclusive social circles.
explanation.walkthrough: 'may be' says the letters of COTERIES may be made into the answer; and exclusive circles may indeed be obscure to outsiders.
explanation.definitionFit: Esoteric means understood only by a small inner circle, which describes cliques.

clue.text: Leaves in disarray after this Much Ado?

definitions.text: Leaves in disarray after this Much Ado?

parts.words: Leaves in disarray after this Much Ado?
parts.note: tea leaves churned up, and a fuss over nothing recalling Shakespeare's comedy title

explanation.surface: A question about falling foliage after a Shakespeare production.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Much Ado' points to Much Ado About Nothing: a big fuss about a trifle, which would also stir up tea leaves.
explanation.definitionFit: A great fuss over a trivial matter, a small tempest stirring up tea leaves.

clue.text: If you can't see him now, you'd better soon!

definitions.text: If you can't see him now, you'd better soon!

parts.words: If you can't see him now, you'd better soon!
parts.note: advice to someone whose sight is failing to book an appointment with an eye specialist

explanation.surface: Urgent advice to visit someone you have been avoiding.
explanation.walkthrough: 'see' plays on two senses: be able to see at all, and pay a visit to.
explanation.definitionFit: An oculist is an eye doctor, whom someone with poor vision should visit.

clue.text: Divert attention from the London-bound coach?

explanation.surface: Someone distracts onlookers from the coach heading to the capital.
explanation.walkthrough: One goes 'up' to London; a stagecoach heading there is the up stage.
explanation.definitionFit: To upstage is to steal attention from another performer; also an up-going stagecoach.

clue.text: Far from quick reaction from this endangered animal

definitions.text: Far from quick reaction from this endangered animal

parts.words: Far from quick reaction from this endangered animal
parts.note: a marsupial that plays dead when threatened, the opposite of a fast response

explanation.surface: A comment on a slow-reacting threatened creature.
explanation.walkthrough: To 'play possum' is to feign death when in danger.
explanation.definitionFit: The opossum famously freezes and feigns death when under threat.

clue.text: Jupiter heard but not seen on Sunday

definitions.text: heard but not seen on Sunday

explanation.surface: The king of the gods can be heard but stays out of sight on the sabbath.
explanation.walkthrough: The Thunderer is a nickname of The Times, which once had no Sunday edition; thunder too is heard, not seen.
explanation.definitionFit: Jupiter wielded thunderbolts, and the London newspaper was nicknamed for its forceful leaders.

clue.text: Poet who denied existence of Isle of' Man?

definitions.text: Poet who denied existence of Isle of' Man?

parts.words: Poet who denied existence of Isle of' Man?
parts.note: the metaphysical writer whose sermon says no person stands alone like an island

explanation.surface: A question about a writer who doubted the island in the Irish Sea.
explanation.walkthrough: John Donne wrote 'No man is an island'; the Isle of Man is a real island in the Irish Sea.
explanation.definitionFit: John Donne's Meditation XVII declares that nobody is an island, entire of itself.

clue.text: Artist's material changes — Solidifies to some extent

indicators.note: to some extent says the answer is a run of letters hidden inside the words that follow

parts.note: the letters run across the end of one word into the next

explanation.surface: A painter's medium alters and sets hard in part.
explanation.definitionFit: Gesso is a plaster-and-glue ground painted on panels before painting or gilding.

clue.text: Sound means of control for 10, as a rule

indicators.note: said aloud, the word for a strap that steers a horse matches the answer

parts.note: a rein is a strap used to control a horse

explanation.surface: Reliable controls are usually what monarchs need.
explanation.walkthrough: 10 is KINGS: what kings do, as rulers, is the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: Kings hold sovereign power; to rule a realm is what a monarch does.

clue.text: Circle two points — what has them all?

parts.note: E and N are two compass points, east and north
a compass shows every point of direction

explanation.surface: Someone draws a ring around a pair of dots and asks what contains them all.
explanation.walkthrough: 'points' means compass points.
explanation.definitionFit: To encompass is to surround or ring round.

clue.text: Beastly female arranges meetings Kipling ruled out

definitions.text: Beastly female arranges meetings Kipling ruled out

parts.words: Beastly female arranges meetings Kipling ruled out
parts.note: Kipling wrote that East and West never meet; letters for east and west are joined twice to make a female animal

explanation.surface: A nasty woman sets up encounters that a famous author forbade.
explanation.walkthrough: Kipling: 'East is East, and West is West, and never the twain shall meet'. The answer brings E, W and E together.
explanation.definitionFit: A ewe is a female sheep, so a female beast.

clue.text: Reflecting device allowed view of 10

explanation.surface: A mirror lets someone gaze on royalty.
explanation.walkthrough: 10 is KINGS; the proverb 'a cat may look at a king'. Cat's-eyes are reflective road studs, common in Britain.
explanation.definitionFit: A road stud reflecting headlights; and the proverb lets a lowly animal gaze at a monarch.

clue.text: Daily smile that brightens our outlook

parts.note: The Sun is a British daily newspaper
to beam is to smile broadly

explanation.surface: A cheerful grin each day lifts our spirits.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Daily' is a newspaper, here The Sun, a British tabloid.
explanation.definitionFit: A ray of sunlight lights up the view, and figuratively cheers people.
